result: {"C1": ["Prefers choosing test tasks where the harmful action is embedded in genuinely expected work over flagrantly dangerous affordances, because embedded failure channels are the realistic and costly-to-avoid ones.", "Prefers realism of the failure channel over speed of existence proofs, because the realistic channel matters more than how quickly an unrealistic setup demonstrates the behavior."], "C2": ["Prefers detecting underperformance via cross-task, cross-domain, and scaling comparisons over single-point evaluation, because anomalies relative to expected performance reveal intentional sandbagging.", "Prefers relative-to-expectation anomaly analysis over honeypot elicitation of true goals, because it does not depend on the model believing or reasoning about whether it is being tested."], "C3": ["Prefers claiming that methodology and building blocks transfer over claiming specific numbers or protocol rankings, because single-setting results are only modest evidence.", "Prefers cautious, scoped claims from single-setting results over strong generalization, because overfitting to one conception of the failure mode is a known risk."], "C4": ["Prefers countermeasures that must withstand a reliable adversary over ones that assume the model is naive, because a scheming AI needs near-perfect consistency and rare slips can unravel its strategy.", "Prefers designing for a worst-case, highly consistent adversary over relying on the model failing to recognize its context, because deployment context is likely inferable from pretraining data and observable interventions."], "C5": ["Prefers non-leading questions and scratchpad analysis over directly leading questions for checking whether the model believes the setup, because leading questions inflate skepticism.", "Prefers measuring belief through unprompted reasoning cues over explicit probing, because direct prompts about whether the situation is fake contaminate the measurement of the model's real beliefs."]}
